title: Two language models can read and change neural networks, but reliability depends on the task
authors: unclear (no author names in the text)

headline_result.text: Repeating seven Sparks tasks with GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 showed task-dependent reliability (car fix 9/10 vs 1/10), and shortcut controls showed every successful car edit also worked on an all-zero network.
headline_result.quote: Claude wrote a successful car controller in 9/10 attempts versus Astra's 1/10; Astra beat weak trained arcade-game networks in 15/15 attempts versus Claude's 13/15.

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: 10-20 attempts per reading/car task, 15 per arcade task, 3 per Go, 1 per math repair

key_claims.claim: Every successful car-repair edit, including the published one, also worked on an all-zero network, so it writes a fixed controller rather than repairing learned behaviour.
key_claims.quote: Every successful edit, including the published one, also worked when applied to a network whose weights were all set to zero. Each edit writes a small fixed controller that overrides the trained network.

key_claims.claim: Game naming from weights follows the training footprint (row lengths) when footprint and function conflict, for both models.
key_claims.quote: Both usually followed the row lengths in the conflict control (Claude 20/20, Astra 19/20).

key_claims.claim: On randomized-weight controls Astra declined to name a game in 19/20 attempts while Claude named one in all 20, though the prompt asserted that the network was trained.
key_claims.quote: On randomized-weight controls, Astra declined to name a game in 19/20 attempts. Claude named a game in all 20 at mean confidence 19%.

key_claims.claim: The original language-identification result may have been exposed by folder names containing the answer; with neutral names Astra got 5 of 12.
key_claims.quote: The original report found Astra correct on both parts in all 6 of its conversations. Its working folders contained language names.

key_claims.claim: Claude's single Qwen3.5-0.8B repair scored 54% on 100 held-out MATH-500 problems versus 49% for Astra's published edit, a difference within noise.
key_claims.quote: On 100 held-out MATH-500 problems, which were kept separate from practice, Claude's edit scored 54% with thinking on, against 49% for Astra's published edit. The paired difference was +5.0 ± 4.1 percentage points

key_claims.claim: The 100-million-step arcade baselines that written networks beat are weak.
key_claims.quote: The 100-million-step baselines are weak: Breakout scores only 15.8, so surpassing that network is a low bar.

limitations_stated.text: Small fixed task set; repeated reads use only a few networks and are not independent.
limitations_stated.quote: Twenty game reads cover four networks, and twelve language reads cover three; repeated reads are not independent network samples.

limitations_stated.text: Analysis choices were partly informed by results; math comparison used unequal budgets and one edit per model.
limitations_stated.quote: The analysis protocol and choice of reliability measures were informed by some of the results. The math comparison used unequal budgets and one edit per model.

limitations_stated.text: One evaluated model (Claude Opus 5.5) wrote the original analysis.
limitations_stated.quote: Claude Opus 5.5, one of the evaluated models, wrote the original analysis; grading was automatic.

notes_for_review: The most systematic multi-task replication of the Sparks report so far: a second editor model, repeated attempts, and shortcut controls (footprint decoy, conflict, randomized weights, all-zero network). Its controls cut against the original interpretation of Exp 1 (game reading follows the footprint) and Exp 4 (car fix is a written controller), and it flags a possible answer leak in the language task. The record includes AI-written reviews (one by Claude Opus 5.5, a compared model) rather than external peer review, and the analysis protocol changed after results; the math arm is a single edit per model and is evaluated on a subset (every fifth MATH-500 problem) in thinking mode, full set in default mode.
